claim: Asthenoteratozoospermia is a prevalent cause of male infertility.
source: Asthenoteratozoospermia, a prevalent cause of male infertility, lacks a well-defined etiology.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation.

claim: DNAH12 is a special dynein featured by the absence of a microtubule-binding domain.
source: DNAH12 is a special dynein featured by the absence of a microtubule-binding domain, however, its functions in spermatogenesis remain largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of DNAH12 in the abstract.

claim: Six biallelic mutations in DNAH12 were identified that co-segregate recessively with male infertility in six distinct families.
source: Through comprehensive genetic analyses involving whole-exome sequencing and subsequent Sanger sequencing on infertile patients and fertile controls from six distinct families, we unveiled six biallelic mutations in DNAH12 that co-segregate recessively with male infertility in the studied families.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic sequencing data presented in the study, including Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy revealed pronounced axonemal abnormalities, including inner dynein arms impairment and central pair loss in sperm flagella of the patients.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed pronounced axonemal abnormalities, including inner dynein arms (IDAs) impairment and central pair (CP) loss in sperm flagella of the patients.
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mouse models (Dnah12-/- and Dnah12mut/mut) recapitulated the reproductive defects in the patients.
source: Mouse models (Dnah12-/- and Dnah12mut/mut) were generated and recapitulated the reproductive defects in the patients.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mouse models shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: DNAH12 deficiency did not show effects on cilium organization and function.
source: Noteworthy, DNAH12 deficiency did not show effects on cilium organization and function.
evidence: This is supported by data showing normal cilia in Dnah12-/- mice in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: DNAH12 was confirmed to interact with two other IDA components DNALI1 and DNAH1.
source: Mechanistically, DNAH12 was confirmed to interact with two other IDA components DNALI1 and DNAH1, while disruption of DNAH12 leads to failed recruitment of DNALI1 and DNAH1 to IDAs and compromised sperm development.
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP experiments shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: Disruption of DNAH12 leads to failed recruitment of DNALI1 and DNAH1 to IDAs and compromised sperm development.
source: Mechanistically, DNAH12 was confirmed to interact with two other IDA components DNALI1 and DNAH1, while disruption of DNAH12 leads to failed recruitment of DNALI1 and DNAH1 to IDAs and compromised sperm development.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7D and 7E showing loss of DNALI1 and DNAH1 signals in Dnah12-/- mice.

claim: DNAH12 interacts with radial spoke head proteins RSPH1, RSPH9, and DNAJB13 to regulate CP stability.
source: Furthermore, DNAH12 also interacts with radial spoke head proteins RSPH1, RSPH9, and DNAJB13 to regulate CP stability.
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data in Figure 8A and expression analysis in Figure 8C.

claim: The infertility of Dnah12-/- mice could be overcome by intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) treatment.
source: Moreover, the infertility of Dnah12-/- mice could be overcome by intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) treatment.
evidence: This is supported by ICSI experimental data shown in Figure 8E-G.

claim: DNAH12 plays a crucial role in the proper organization of axoneme in sperm flagella, but not cilia, by recruiting DNAH1 and DNALI1 in both humans and mice.
source: Collectively, DNAH12 plays a crucial role in the proper organization of axoneme in sperm flagella, but not cilia, by recruiting DNAH1 and DNALI1 in both humans and mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings throughout the study.

claim: Infertility impacts around 8–12% of couples during their reproductive years.
source: Infertility has emerged as a global health concern, impacting around 8–12% of couples during their reproductive years, approximately 50% of infertility cases are attributed to male factors (Agarwal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agarwal et al., 2021.

claim: Approximately 50% of infertility cases are attributed to male factors.
source: Infertility has emerged as a global health concern, impacting around 8–12% of couples during their reproductive years, approximately 50% of infertility cases are attributed to male factors (Agarwal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agarwal et al., 2021.

claim: Asthenoteratozoospermia is characterized by poor sperm motility and notable morphological abnormalities.
source: Among these, asthenoteratozoospermia, characterized by poor sperm motility and notable morphological abnormalities, stands out as a prevalent contributor to male infertility (Krausz and Riera-Escamilla, 2018; Shang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krausz and Riera-Escamilla, 2018 and Shang et al., 2018.

claim: Multiple gene mutations have been associated with asthenoteratozoospermia and male infertility, including DNAH1, DNAH2, DNAH6, DNAH7, DNAH10, DNAH8, and DNAH17.
source: Recent investigations have unveiled a multitude of gene mutations associated with asthenoteratozoospermia and male infertility, including Dynein Axonemal Heavy Chain (DNAH) inner dynein arm (IDA) genes like DNAH1, DNAH2, DNAH6, DNAH7, and DNAH10, as well as outer dynein arm (ODA) genes such as DNAH8 and DNAH17, all implicated in primary male infertility with asthenoteratozoospermia (Khan et al., 2021; Li et al., 2019; Tu et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2022a; Li et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020; Whitfield et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Genes encoding cilia and flagella-associated proteins (CFAP), including CFAP43, CFAP44, CFAP57, and CFAP61, have been identified as linked to asthenoteratozoospermia.
source: Additionally, genes encoding cilia and flagella-associated proteins (CFAP), including CFAP43, CFAP44, CFAP57, and CFAP61, have been identified as linked to asthenoteratozoospermia (Coutton et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: The axoneme exhibits a well-organized pattern with nine peripheral doublet microtubules (DMTs) and a central pair of microtubules (CP), constituting the classical '9+2' microtubular arrangement.
source: The axoneme, a fundamental structure of cilia and flagella, exhibits a well-organized pattern with nine peripheral doublet microtubules (DMTs) and a central pair of microtubules (CP), constituting the classical '9+2' microtubular arrangement (Touré et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Touré et al., 2021.

claim: The radial spoke (RS) head contacts the CP accessory structures, transmitting mechanical and chemical signals from the central microtubules to the axonemal dynein arms.
source: In motile cilia or flagella, the radial spoke (RS) head contacts the CP accessory structures, transmitting mechanical and chemical signals from the central microtubules to the axonemal dynein arms, thus coordinating the flagellar or ciliary movement (Walton et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walton et al., 2023.

claim: The DNAH family in mammalian species includes eight IDA members (DNAH1-3, DNAH6, DNAH7, DNAH10, DNAH12, DNAH14) and five ODA members (DNAH5, DNAH8, DNAH9, DNAH11, DNAH17).
source: Within mammalian species, the DNAH family plays a crucial role in the axonemal structure, encompassing eight IDA members (DNAH1-3, DNAH6, DNAH7, DNAH10, DNAH12, DNAH14) and five ODA members (DNAH5, DNAH8, DNAH9, DNAH11, DNAH17).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the DNAH family.

claim: Chlamydomonas ODAs primarily regulate beat frequency, while IDAs contribute to bending formation and beating form.
source: Chlamydomonas ODAs, composed of α, β, and γ chains, primarily regulate beat frequency, while IDAs, with seven major subspecies (a-g), contribute to bending formation and beating form (Viswanadha et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Viswanadha et al., 2017.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding ODA or IDA components have been linked to asthenoteratozoospermia, with or without symptoms of primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD).
source: Mutations in genes encoding ODA or IDA components have been linked to asthenoteratozoospermia, with or without symptoms of primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), a genetic disorder characterized by chronic airway infections or situs inversus (Kleinboelting et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kleinboelting et al., 2014.

claim: Deficiency in DNAH7 or DNAH11 may lead to PCD.
source: Notably, deficiency in certain IDAs and ODAs coding genes, such as DNAH7 or DNAH11, may lead to PCD (Shoemark et al., 2018; Sironen et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shoemark et al., 2018; Sironen et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2021.

claim: Patients carrying mutations in DNAH1 and DNAH2 typically lack PCD symptoms.
source: Patients carrying mutations in DNAH1 and DNAH2 typically lack PCD symptoms (Khan et al., 2021), although a study suggested the potential contribution of the DNAH1 p.Lys1154Gln mutation to PCD (Imtiaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Khan et al., 2021 and Imtiaz et al., 2015.

claim: DNAH12 is the shortest member and lacks a typical microtubule-binding domain (MTBD) in the DNAH family.
source: Notably, it is the shortest member and lacks a typical microtubule-binding domain (MTBD) in the DNAH family.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of DNAH12.

claim: Mutations of DNAH12 have been predicted to be associated with male patients' infertility, however, limited pathogenic evidence was provided, and the underlying pathogenesis remained unclear.
source: Mutations of DNAH12 have been predicted to be associated with male patients' infertility, however, limited pathogenic evidence was provided, and the underlying pathogenesis remained unclear (Li et al., 2021; Oud et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2021 and Oud et al., 2021.

claim: DNAH12 mRNA is predominantly detected in trachea and testis.
source: Besides, although DNAH12 has been identified as a possible axonemal dynein and its mRNA is predominantly detected in two tissues containing axonemal structures: trachea and testis (Vaisberg et al., 1996; Chapelin et al., 1997), its physiological functions remain largely elusive.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vaisberg et al., 1996 and Chapelin et al., 1997.

claim: 796 infertile patients from unrelated Pakistani and Chinese families diagnosed with asthenozoospermia were enrolled in this study.
source: In this study, we enrolled 796 infertile patients from unrelated Pakistani and Chinese families diagnosed with asthenozoospermia.
evidence: This describes the study cohort.

claim: All seven variants identified in DNAH12 were rare in public human genome databases, including the 1000 Genome Project and gnomAD (v3).
source: All seven variants were rare in public human genome databases, including the 1000 Genome Project and gnomAD (v3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1 showing allele frequencies.

claim: The identified DNAH12 variants were predicted to be deleterious by in-silico software tools such as SIFT, Polyphen2, fathmm-MKL, and CADD2.
source: Additionally, these variants were predicted to be deleterious by in-silico software tools such as SIFT, Polyphen2, fathmm-MKL, and CADD2 (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by computational predictions shown in Table 1.

claim: DNAH12 mRNA and protein showed high expression in testes and relatively lower expression in lungs and tracheas of male mice and oviducts of female mice.
source: Experimentally, our RT-PCR, qPCR, and immunoblotting detection of DNAH12 expression in different tissues indicated that both DNAH12 mRNA and protein showed high expression in testes and relatively lower expression in lungs and tracheas of male mice and oviducts of female mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: DNAH12 protein was initially detected in testes around 21 d postpartum (dpp) and thereafter maintained a high level.
source: Furthermore, DNAH12 protein was initially detected in testes around 21 d postpartum (dpp) and thereafter maintained a high level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: DNAH12 is conservative from Chlamydomonas to humans.
source: Further phylogenetic analysis revealed the conservative nature of DNAH12 from Chlamydomonas to humans (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: All the amino acids affected by mutations were conserved in mammals and were located in functional regions, including the ATPase domains or the Stem domain of DNAH12.
source: All the amino acids affected by mutations were conserved in mammals and were located in functional regions, including the ATPase domains or the Stem domain of DNAH12 (Figure 1C), indicating that these mutations are highly likely to hinder the structure, function, or stability of the DNAH12 protein.
evidence: This is supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All affected individuals exhibited significantly reduced sperm motility and progressive motility.
source: All affected individuals exhibited significantly reduced sperm motility and progressive motility (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by clinical data shown in Table 2.

claim: Spermatozoa from the patients exhibited a range of abnormal morphologies, including short, coiled, absent, bent, or irregular caliber flagella, accompanied by aberrant heads.
source: Spermatozoa from fertile controls displayed normal heads and tails, while spermatozoa from the patients exhibited a range of abnormal morphologies, including short, coiled, absent, bent, or irregular caliber flagella, accompanied by aberrant heads (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The predicted DNAH12 protein size was detected in the sperm lysate from a fertile control but not in P9, P10, and P11.
source: The predicted DNAH12 protein size was detected in the sperm lysate from a fertile control but not in P9 with the homozygous stop-gain mutation M4, P10 with a homozygous missense mutation M5, and P11 with compound heterozygous mutations M6 and M7, indicating these mutations possibly lead to the disruption of the DNAH12 protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DNAH12 signals were localized along the flagella of the fertile control, however, no DNAH12 signals were observed in sperm flagella of patients P3, P5, P8, P9, P10, and P11.
source: The results showed that DNAH12 signals were localized along the flagella of the fertile control, however, no DNAH12 signals were observed in sperm flagella of patients P3 (family 1), P5 (family 2), P8 (family 3), P9, P10, and P11 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Various defects were found in patients' sperm flagella, including loss of CP (54.5%), disorganization of microtubules (26%), and absence of DMTs (16.5%) in the examined cross-sections.
source: In contrast, various defects were found in our patients, including loss of CP (54.5%), disorganization of microtubules (26%), and absence of DMTs (16.5%) in the examined cross-sections (Figure 3A, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3A, C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Approximately 70% of sections examined showed impaired IDA structures in the analyzed three patients.
source: Compared with axonemes in controls that almost all the sections presented intact IDAs, approximately 70% of sections examined showed impaired IDA structures in the analyzed three patients (Figure 3B, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3B, D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The sperm flagella of patients showed remarkably reduced SPAG6 signals when compared with those from controls.
source: The sperm flagella of patients showed remarkably reduced SPAG6 signals when compared with those from controls (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: DNAH1 and DNALI1 signals were both obviously decreased in the patients' sperm flagella.
source: Similarly, DNAH1 and DNALI1 signals were both obviously decreased in the patients' sperm flagella, indicating impaired IDAs in the patients (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: DNAH17 and ODF2 signals in patients' flagella were comparable to those in a normal control.
source: Besides, DNAH17 and ODF2 signals in patients' flagella were comparable to those in a normal control (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Dnah12-/- males exhibited normal development but were infertile.
source: Dnah12-/- males exhibited normal development but were infertile (Figure 4A), while Dnah12-/- female mice showed normal development and fertility, and no obvious defective oviductal and tracheal cilia (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by fertility test data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Dnah12-/- female mice showed normal development and fertility, and no obvious defective oviductal and tracheal cilia.
source: Dnah12-/- males exhibited normal development but were infertile (Figure 4A), while Dnah12-/- female mice showed normal development and fertility, and no obvious defective oviductal and tracheal cilia (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by fertility test data and histology shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The body weight of Dnah12-/- and Dnah12+/+ males was comparable, while smaller testes were observed in Dnah12-/- males.
source: The body weight of Dnah12-/- and Dnah12+/+ males was comparable, while smaller testes were observed in Dnah12-/- males (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The average number of sperm per epididymis of Dnah12-/- mice dramatically decreased to approximately 2% of that of Dnah12+/+ mice.
source: Besides, the average number of sperm per epididymis of Dnah12-/- mice dramatically decreased to approximately 2% of that of Dnah12+/+ mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by sperm count data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The epididymal caudal spermatozoa of Dnah12-/- male mice were 100% immotile.
source: The epididymal caudal spermatozoa of Dnah12-/- male mice were 100% immotile, compared to those of Dnah12+/+ mice (Figure 4D, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by motility data shown in Figure 4D and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Morphological analysis of sperm from the caudal epididymis of Dnah12-/- mice showed similar types and frequencies of flagellum and head abnormalities to those observed in patients.
source: Importantly, morphological analysis of sperm from the caudal epididymis of Dnah12-/- mice showed similar types and frequencies of flagellum and head abnormalities to those observed in our patients (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The manchette structure in Dnah12-/- was roughly normal until steps 9–10 (Stage IX-X) but was aberrantly stretched from steps 11–12 (Stage XI-XII) when compared with those of Dnah12+/+ mice.
source: The manchette structure in Dnah12-/- was roughly normal until steps 9–10 (Stage IX-X) but was aberrantly stretched from steps 11–12 (Stage XI-XII) when compared with those of Dnah12+/+ mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: TEM analysis showed severely abnormal head morphology in elongated spermatids of Dnah12-/- males when compared with those of Dnah12+/+ males.
source: TEM analysis showed severely abnormal head morphology in elongated spermatids of Dnah12-/- males when compared with those of Dnah12+/+ males (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: TUNEL assays of testis sections showed dramatically increased proportions of seminiferous tubules containing TUNEL-positive cells in Dnah12-/- mice, compared with those in Dnah12+/+ mice.
source: Additionally, TUNEL assays of testis sections showed dramatically increased proportions of seminiferous tubules containing TUNEL-positive cells in Dnah12-/- mice, compared with those in Dnah12+/+ mice, suggesting the aberrant spermatids may undergo apoptosis (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 4K–M.

claim: Sperm from Dnah12-/- mice exhibited severe abnormalities in all the analyzed sections, characterized by CP loss and disorganized axoneme structure.
source: In contrast, sperm from Dnah12-/- mice exhibited severe abnormalities in all the analyzed sections, characterized by CP loss and disorganized axoneme structure (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Dnah12-/- sperm showed a significant reduction in the abundance of DNAH1 and DNALI1, while the amount of DNAI2 remained comparable to Dnah12+/+ and Dnah12+/- sperm.
source: Immunoblotting was performed to assess the expression levels of DNAH1, DNALI1, and SPAG6 in sperm lysates, Dnah12-/- sperm showed a significant reduction in the abundance of DNAH1 and DNALI1, while the amount of DNAI2 (a component of ODAs) remained comparable to Dnah12+/+ and Dnah12+/- sperm (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Immunofluorescence assays revealed the near absence of signals for SPAG6, SPEF2, DNAH1, and DNALI1 in Dnah12-/- sperm flagella, whereas DNAH17 and DNAI2 remained unaffected.
source: Additionally, immunofluorescence assays revealed the near absence of signals for SPAG6, SPEF2 (a component of CP complex), DNAH1, and DNALI1 in Dnah12-/- sperm flagella, whereas DNAH17 and DNAI2 (components of ODAs) remained unaffected (Figure 5C–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C–H.

claim: Both Dnah12mut/mut and Dnah12-/- males developed normally and showed no tracheal motility or structure defects.
source: Intriguingly, both Dnah12mut/mut and Dnah12-/- males developed normally and showed no tracheal motility or structure defects, despite the expression of DNAH12 being detected in tracheal cilia cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–E; Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by histology and video data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–E and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: The ultra-structures of cilia axonemes were comparable in wild-type and Dnah12-/- groups.
source: Besides, the ultra-structures of cilia axonemes were comparable in wild-type and Dnah12-/- groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3F.

claim: DNAH12 is a distinctive IDA lacking the microtubule-binding domain (MTBD).
source: Through phylogenetic and domain analyses of DNAH family members, we found that DNAH12 is a distinctive IDA lacking the microtubule-binding domain (MTBD), which is crucial for ATP-sensitive microtubule binding and motor direction control (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and domain analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Potential interactors of DNAH12 were mainly enriched in motor protein, actin binding, myosin and RNA binding proteins.
source: Gene ontology analysis showed that the potential interactors were mainly enriched in motor protein, actin binding, myosin and RNA binding proteins (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Potential IDA interactors such as DNALI1, DNAH1, DNAH3, and DNAH2 were co-enriched in the candidate interacting dynein protein list.
source: Besides the predominant enrichment of DNAH12 (top1), potential IDA interactors such as DNALI1 (top2), DNAH1 (top3), DNAH3 (top4), and DNAH2 (top5) were co-enriched in the candidate interacting dynein protein list (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Immunoblotting confirmed the co-enrichment of DNAH12, DNALI1, and DNAH1 in the immunoprecipitated complex by the DNAH12 rabbit antibody in Dnah12+/+ mice but not in Dnah12-/- mice.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed the co-enrichment of DNAH12, DNALI1, and DNAH1 in the immunoprecipitated complex by the DNAH12 rabbit antibody in Dnah12+/+ mice but not in Dnah12-/- mice, indicating specific interactions between DNAH12 and DNALI1, DNAH1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Reciprocal in vivo Co-IP using an anti-DNALI1 antibody further validated strong interactions among DNAH12, DNALI1, and DNAH1.
source: Reciprocal in vivo Co-IP using an anti-DNALI1 antibody further validated strong interactions among these three IDA components (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The N-terminal Stem domain of DNAH12 possibly interacts with DNALI1 in the top three best-fit conformations.
source: Employing Phyre2, we constructed the structural models of both proteins and further elucidated their interaction dynamics via DNAH12-DNALI1 docking using the HDOCK server. The results showed that the N-terminal Stem domain of DNAH12 possibly interacts with DNALI1 in the top three best-fit conformations (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by protein docking analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: In vitro Co-IP assays validated that the Stem domain of DNAH12 indeed mediates interactions with DNALI1.
source: Considering DNAH12 is encoded by 3092 amino acids and their full-length protein interactions have been proved in vivo, we constructed the Stem domain (1–1212 amino acids) of DNAH12 and full-length DNALI1 plasmid, further in vitro Co-IP assays validated that the Stem domain of DNAH12 indeed mediates interactions with DNALI1 (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro Co-IP data shown in Figure 6H–J.

claim: The protein levels of DNALI1 and DNAH1 were decreased in Dnah12-/- testes, while the level of ODA member DNAI1 was comparable.
source: To evaluate the effect of DNAH12 deletion on DNALI1 and DNAH1 during spermiogenesis, we examined the abundance of the DNAH12 interaction partners, DNALI1 and DNAH1, in Dnah12+/+ and Dnah12-/- mouse testis lysate. The protein levels of DNALI1 and DNAH1 were decreased in Dnah12-/- testes, while the level of ODA member DNAI1 was comparable (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The signals of DNALI1 or DNAH1 in round spermatids of Dnah12-/- mice were comparable to those of Dnah12+/+ mice.
source: Although the signals of DNALI1 or DNAH1 in round spermatids of Dnah12-/- mice were comparable to those of Dnah12+/+ mice (Figure 7B and C), the recruitment of DNALI1 and DNAH1 to sperm flagella was severely impaired in elongated spermatids of Dnah12-/- mice (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: The recruitment of DNALI1 and DNAH1 to sperm flagella was severely impaired in elongated spermatids of Dnah12-/- mice.
source: Although the signals of DNALI1 or DNAH1 in round spermatids of Dnah12-/- mice were comparable to those of Dnah12+/+ mice (Figure 7B and C), the recruitment of DNALI1 and DNAH1 to sperm flagella was severely impaired in elongated spermatids of Dnah12-/- mice (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: DNALI1 and DNAH1 were comparable in the oviduct and trachea of Dnah12+/+ and Dnah12-/- groups.
source: We thus checked the abundance of DNALI1 and DNAH1 in the oviduct and trachea, the results showed that DNALI1 and DNAH1 were comparable in the Dnah12+/+ and Dnah12-/- groups (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: No discernible disparities were observed in the intensity and localization of DNALI1 and DNAH1 signals within the oviduct and trachea of Dnah12+/+ and Dnah12-/- mice.
source: Furthermore, no discernible disparities were observed in the intensity and localization of DNALI1 and DNAH1 signals within the oviduct and trachea (Figure 7H–K).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7H–K.

claim: In patients with DNALI1 deficiency, flagellar DNAH1 but not DNAH12 signals were absent.
source: In patients and mice with DNALI1 deficiency, flagellar DNAH1 but not DNAH12 signals were absent (Wu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2023.

claim: In comparison to those in the control, the DNALI1 signals were absent, while no discernible differences in DNAH12 signals were observed in the flagella of the patient with the DNAH1 mutation.
source: In comparison to those in the control, the DNALI1 signals were absent, while no discernible differences in DNAH12 signals were observed in the flagella of the patient with the DNAH1 mutation (Figure 7N and O).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7N and O.

claim: Clusters of RS head-related proteins such as RSPH1, RSPH9, or DNAJB13 were enriched in the testicular interactome of DNAH12.
source: In addition to the enrichment of dynein proteins, we noticed that clusters of RS head-related proteins such as RSPH1, RSPH9, or DNAJB13 were enriched in the testicular interactome of DNAH12.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data from the DNAH12 interactome.

claim: Deficiency in RSPH1, RSPH9, or DNAJB13 were associated with CP loss phenotype.
source: Considering that deficiency in RSPH1 (Lin et al., 2014), RSPH9 (Zhu et al., 2019), or DNAJB13 (Liu et al., 2022) were associated with CP loss phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022.

claim: Co-IP results proved the interactions of RSPH1, RSPH9, and DNAJB13 with DNAH12 in the testis.
source: We then explored their interaction with DNAH12 in the testis lysate, the results proved the interactions of these proteins with DNAH12 in the testis (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: AlphaFold3 analyses showed that RSPH1, RSPH9, and DNAJB13 may interact with DNAH12 through the Stem domain.
source: Further analyses by AlphaFold3 showed that these proteins may interacts with DNAH12 through the Stem domain (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by AlphaFold3 analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The expression of RSPH1, RSPH9, and DNAJB13 showed an obvious decrease in testis lysate of Dnah12-/- mice.
source: The expression of RSPH1, RSPH9, and DNAJB13 showed an obvious decrease in testis lysate of Dnah12-/- mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Immunofluorescence assays revealed the loss of signals for RSPH1 in Dnah12-/- sperm flagella.
source: Additionally, immunofluorescence assays revealed the loss of signals for RSPH1, a marker of RS head, in Dnah12-/- sperm flagella (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The percentages of 2-cell and blastocyst-stage embryos in Dnah12-/- group showed no difference compared to those of Dnah12+/+ group after ICSI.
source: Promisingly, the percentages of 2-cell and blastocyst-stage embryos in Dnah12-/- group showed no difference compared to those of Dnah12+/+ group (Figure 8E–G), indicating that ICSI could also be an effective treatment for infertile men carrying DNAH12 variants.
evidence: This is supported by ICSI experimental data shown in Figure 8E–G.

claim: DNAH12 interacts with DNALI1 and DNAH1, and this interaction is a prerequisite for the proper localization of DNALI1 and DNAH1 to sperm flagella.
source: Taken together, we suggest that DNAH12 interacts with DNALI1 and DNAH1, and this interaction is a prerequisite for the proper localization of DNALI1 and DNAH1 to sperm flagella, which is essential for the intact IDAs and CP structures in both humans and mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: DNALI1 and DNAH1 exhibit mutual dependence for their localization to sperm flagella.
source: Additionally, DNALI1 and DNAH1 exhibit mutual dependence for their localization to sperm flagella.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of either protein affects the other's localization.

claim: Deficiency of DNAH12 leads to the failure of DNALI1 and DNAH1 recruitment to sperm flagella, resulting in abnormal sperm morphology characterized by compromised axoneme organization, causing male infertility.
source: Deficiency of DNAH12 leads to the failure of DNALI1 and DNAH1 recruitment to sperm flagella, resulting in abnormal sperm morphology characterized by compromised axoneme organization, causing male infertility (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 8H.

claim: The assembly of IDA components occurs intricately, possibly not synchronously in time and space.
source: Moreover, our results indicate that the assembly of IDA components occurs intricately, possibly not synchronously in time and space.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of DNAH12, DNALI1, and DNAH1 deficiencies.

claim: Dnah12-/- males have more severe phenotypes than Dnali1 and Dnah1 knockout mice, including a more severe reduced sperm count (~2% of normal values).
source: Notably, Dnah12-/- mice exhibit more severe phenotypes than Dnali1 and Dnah1 knockout mice (Khan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023; Yap et al., 2023), including a more severe reduced sperm count (~2% of normal values), this observation further supports our perspective.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data from cited studies (Khan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023; Yap et al., 2023) and data from this study.

claim: Deficiency of DNAH12 potential partner DNAH1 presents quite similar defects with DNAH12, indicating DNAH12 and DNAH1 possibly exhibit synergic functions in axonemal proper arrangement.
source: Noteworthy, deficiency of DNAH12 potential partner DNAH1, a well-known asthenoteratozoospermia-related gene, presents quite similar defects with DNAH12, indicating DNAH12 and DNAH1 possibly exhibit synergic functions in axonemal proper arrangement (Ben Khelifa et al., 2014; Wambergue et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ben Khelifa et al., 2014; Wambergue et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2023.

claim: Deficiency in DNAH2 or DNAH6 also leads to high proportions of CP loss and disorganized axonemal structures.
source: In addition to DNAH12 and DNAH1, deficiency in DNAH2 or DNAH6 also leads to high proportions of CP loss and disorganized axonemal structures (Li et al., 2019; Hwang et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2019; Hwang et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021.

claim: DNALI1, DNAH7, or DNAH10 deficiency results in no obvious CP loss but impaired IDA integrity.
source: However, DNALI1, DNAH7, or DNAH10 deficiency results in no obvious CP loss but impaired IDA integrity (Gao et al., 2022a; Li et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2022a; Li et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023.

claim: Specific IDA components, like DNAH12 and DNAH1, are required for the maintenance of CP integrity.
source: These studies indicate that specific IDA components, like DNAH12 and DNAH1, are required for the maintenance of CP integrity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deficiency in these proteins leads to CP loss.

claim: Multiple dynein proteins are produced to support the intricate organization of sperm flagella.
source: Moreover, discrepancies observed in the phenotypes resulting from deficiencies in specific IDAs suggest that multiple dynein proteins are produced to support the intricate organization of sperm flagella.
evidence: This is inferred from the diverse phenotypes observed with different dynein deficiencies.

claim: DNAH12, and other IDAs, possibly regulate the stability of CP through the cooperation with RS head proteins.
source: Noteworthy, deficiency in RS head proteins RSPH1, RSPH9, or DNAJB13 were related to axonemal CP loss phenotype (Lin et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2020), indicating that DNAH12, and other IDAs, possibly regulate the stability of CP through the cooperation with RS head proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the interaction data and the similar CP loss phenotypes.

claim: DNAH12 is initially expressed in the cytoplasm of the round spermatid, while it's enriched in the manchette structure of the elongating spermatid and the tail of the elongated spermatid.
source: The localization of DNAH12 presents dynamic changes during spermiogenesis. DNAH12 is initially expressed in the cytoplasm of the round spermatid, while it's enriched in the manchette structure of the elongating spermatid and the tail of the elongated spermatid.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence observations during spermiogenesis.

claim: The manchette and the sperm tail axoneme are two microtubular platforms that transport proteins to the developing head and tail.
source: The manchette and the sperm tail axoneme are two microtubular platforms that transport proteins to the developing head and tail (Lehti and Sironen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lehti and Sironen, 2016.

claim: Manchette is a transient skirt-like structure and functions as a scaffold for morphological remodeling, contributing to the formation of the sperm head, neck, and tail.
source: Manchette is a transient skirt-like structure and functions as a scaffold for morphological remodeling, contributing to the formation of the sperm head, neck, and tail (Hu et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2023b.

claim: DNAH12 deficiency results in abnormal manchette structure and compromised sperm head and tail morphology.
source: Here, we found that DNAH12 deficiency results in abnormal manchette structure and compromised sperm head and tail morphology.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and TEM data in Figure 4.

claim: In sperm of Dnah12-/- males, several CP complex proteins like SPAG6, and SPEF2 are not properly assembled and the axoneme structure of the tail was severely disorganized.
source: Additionally, in sperm of Dnah12-/- males, several CP complex proteins like SPAG6, and SPEF2 are not properly assembled and the axoneme structure of the tail was severely disorganized, indicating dynein components are responsible for proper axonemal components organization.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5.

claim: DNALI1 showed similar localization patterns to DNAH12.
source: Noteworthy, DNALI1, a potential DNAH12 interacting partner showed similar localization patterns to DNAH12, a study presented that DNALI1 recruits and stabilizes manchette component PACRG, and DNALI1 deficiency causes impaired sperm flagellar assembly (Yap et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yap et al., 2023.

claim: Dynein proteins like DNAH12 and DNALI, possibly work together in the manchette organization as well as sperm flagellar components assembly during sperm development.
source: These data hint that dynein proteins like DNAH12 and DNALI, possibly work together in the manchette organization as well as sperm flagellar components assembly during sperm development.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar localization patterns and phenotypes.

claim: None of the patients carrying bi-allelic DNAH12 mutations claimed symptoms of PCD via visits except for the reproductive problems.
source: Besides, none of the patients carrying bi-allelic DNAH12 mutations claimed symptoms of PCD via visits except for the reproductive problems.
evidence: This is based on clinical information from patient visits.

claim: The mother (III:2) of patients from family 2, carrying homozygous DNAH12 mutation M2 had 6 offspring.
source: Dnah12-/- female mice showed normal development and fertility and the mother (III:2) of patients from family 2, carrying homozygous DNAH12 mutation M2 had 6 offspring.
evidence: This is based on family history data.

claim: The localization and abundance of DNALI1 and DNAH1 in oviductal or tracheal cilia were not affected after Dnah12 deletion.
source: Intriguingly, we found that the localization and abundance of DNALI1 and DNAH1 in oviductal or tracheal cilia were not affected after Dnah12 deletion, indicating that DNAH12 works differently in flagella and cilia.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and immunoblotting data in Figure 7.

claim: Deficiency of specific DNAH members like DNAH6, or DNAH7, but not DNAH2, results in PCD symptoms.
source: Deficiency of specific DNAH members like DNAH6 (Li et al., 2016), or DNAH7 (Wei et al., 2021), but not DNAH2 (Hwang et al., 2021), results in PCD symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2021.

claim: DNAH family members possibly present disparate processing of axonemal biogenesis and organization through evolution in flagella and cilia.
source: Hence, DNAH family members possibly present disparate processing of axonemal biogenesis and organization through evolution in flagella and cilia, further explorations could contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the differences between flagella and cilia, and personalized clinical diagnosis of related diseases like male/female infertility and/or PCD (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of DNAH deficiencies in flagella versus cilia.

claim: Two genetic screening studies mentioned unverified compound heterozygous mutations and a homozygous missense mutation in DNAH12, predicting their association with patients' infertility.
source: Previously, two genetic screening studies mentioned unverified compound heterozygous mutations and a homozygous missense mutation in DNAH12, predicting their association with patients' infertility. However, limited genetic evidence was provided, and the pathogenesis remained unclear (Li et al., 2021; Oud et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2021 and Oud et al., 2021.

claim: Patients carrying mutations in DNAH17 have poor ICSI outcomes.
source: Previous studies have shown that patients carrying mutations in DNAH17 Whitfield et al., 2019 have poor ICSI outcomes while patients with DNAH1(59), DNAH2 (Li et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2021), DNAH3 (Meng et al., 2024), DNAH7 (Wei et al., 2021), or DNAH8 (Weng et al., 2021) mutations have achieved favorable clinical pregnancy.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Whitfield et al., 2019.

claim: Patients with DNAH1, DNAH2, DNAH3, DNAH7, or DNAH8 mutations have achieved favorable clinical pregnancy with ICSI.
source: Previous studies have shown that patients carrying mutations in DNAH17 Whitfield et al., 2019 have poor ICSI outcomes while patients with DNAH1(59), DNAH2 (Li et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2021), DNAH3 (Meng et al., 2024), DNAH7 (Wei et al., 2021), or DNAH8 (Weng et al., 2021) mutations have achieved favorable clinical pregnancy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The successful ICSI outcomes of Dnah12-/- mice suggest that ICSI could be used as a potential treatment for infertile men carrying Dnah12 mutations.
source: In our study, the successful ICSI outcomes of Dnah12-/- mice suggest that ICSI could be used as a potential treatment for infertile men carrying Dnah12 mutations.
evidence: This is based on ICSI experimental data from Dnah12-/- mice.
